en: Cūḷaniddesa:
Exposition of the Pārāyaṇa Chapter;
Exposition of the Questions.
9. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Todeyya:
"In whom desires do not dwell," [said the Venerable Todeyya].
For one in whom craving no longer exists,
who has crossed over all doubt—
what kind of liberation is his?
"In whom sensual desires do not dwell" means: in whom sensual desires do not dwell, do not cohabit, do not reside, do not remain—in whom sensual desires do not dwell.
Thus spoke the Venerable Todeyya.
“Thus” (*iccā*) is a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhi*) ... [etc. ... this refers to the sequential order of the words (*padānupubbatā*).
“Venerable” (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment ... [etc. ...
"Todeyya" is the name of that brahmin... [and so on] ...the designation—thus spoke the Venerable Todeyya.
"In whom craving does not exist": for whom craving is not found, does not exist, is not present, and is not obtained, being burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
He in whom craving does not exist.

"And he who has crossed over doubt": he who has crossed over doubt, crossed beyond, gone beyond, transcended, fully transcended, and passed beyond—it is thus that one is said to have "crossed over doubt."

"What is his liberation like? means: "What is his liberation like? Of what shape, of what kind, and of what appearance should it be desired? Thus he asks about liberation—"What is his liberation like?
Therefore that brahmin said:
“In whom sensual desires do not dwell,
(so said the Venerable Todeyya,) and in whom craving is no longer found;”
“And for one who has crossed over doubt,
what is his liberation like?
“In whom sensual desires do not dwell,”
"Toḍeyya," said the Blessed One,
"is one in whom craving no longer exists,
who has crossed over all doubt."
"For him there is no further liberation.
"In whom desires do not dwell" means:
in which person, in the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
Regarding sensual pleasures (*kāma*): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures—sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*).
… [as follows] … these are called sensual pleasures as objects. … [as follows] …
These are called the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāmā*).
"In whom sensual desires do not dwell" means: in whom sensual desires do not dwell, do not cohabit, do not inhabit, and do not reside—in whom sensual desires do not dwell.
"Todeyya, O Blessed One.
"Todeyya," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a term of reverence... [as before] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One."
"He shall die," said the Blessed One.
"In whom craving no longer exists.
Craving means craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
“Of whom” means of the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.

“In whom craving does not exist” means that for whom craving does not exist, is not present, is not found, is not obtained; it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed; it is incapable of arising again, being burnt up by the fire of knowledge—thus, “in whom craving does not exist.”
"And one who has crossed over doubt": "doubt" (kathaṅkathā) is said to be perplexity (vicikicchā).
It is uncertainty regarding suffering... [and so on] ...it is trepidation and mental distress.
"One who": he who is an Arhat, whose taints are exhausted.

"And one who has crossed over doubt": he who has crossed over doubt, crossed beyond, crossed over completely, transcended, fully transcended, and passed beyond—it is thus "one who has crossed over doubt.
"There is no further liberation for him": there is no other liberation remaining for him.
By whatever liberation one might be liberated, one is liberated;
for such a person, what is to be done has been accomplished by that liberation—
there is no further liberation for them.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“In whom sensual desires do not dwell,
(O Todeyya, said the Blessed One)”
For one in whom craving no longer exists,
who has crossed over all doubt—
there is for him no further liberation.
Free from longing yet appearing to have longings,
wise yet appearing to be merely fashioning wisdom—
how, O Sakka, may I truly recognize such a sage?
Explain that to me, O All-Seeing One:
Is he one who has no longing, or is he one who still longs? Is he free from craving, or does he still crave forms, sounds...
smells... [and so on]...?
In tastes … in tangibles … in clans …
The group … the residence … the gain …
fame … praise … happiness …
robes … almsfood … lodgings …
the requisite of medicinal supplies as a support for the sick … the sense-sphere realm … the fine-material realm …
the formless realm … sensual existence … fine-material existence …
the formless existence … the percipient existence … the non-percipient existence …
the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception … the one-aggregate existence … the four-aggregate existence …
the five-aggregate existence … past … future …
"He hankers after, relishes, yearns for, longs for, and craves present phenomena— and those things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—
thus he is one who has no hope, yet is full of hope."
"Is he one who possesses wisdom, or is he a fabricator of wisdom?
"One who possesses wisdom" (*paññāṇavā*) means one who is wise, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. "But is he a fabricator of wisdom?

(*uda paññakappī*): Does he, by means of the knowledge of the eight attainments, or the knowledge of the five higher powers, or even wrong knowledge, fashion, generate, produce, bring about, or fully manifest either a fabrication of craving or a fabrication of views? Thus it is asked.
"One who possesses wisdom or one who fashions wisdom—
how may I know such a sage, O Sakka?
"Sakka" refers to the Blessed One, Sakka.
He is called Sakka because he went forth from the Sakya clan;
or alternatively, he is called Sakka because he is wealthy, possessing great riches and abundant wealth.
His riches are as follows: namely—

The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of moral dread, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of the foundations of mindfulness,
the wealth of the right efforts, the wealth of the bases of psychic power, the wealth of the faculties, the wealth of the powers, the wealth of the factors of enlightenment,
the wealth of the path, the wealth of the fruits, and the wealth of Nibbāna.
He is called Sakka because he is rich, possessed of great wealth, and wealthy through those many kinds of treasures and jewels;

or alternatively, he is called Sakka because he is powerful, a lord, self-reliant, capable, heroic, valiant, resolute, fearless, undaunted, not terrified, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and being free from horripilation.
“Sakka, how may I know the sage? means: Sakka, how may I know the sage, understand him, discern him, penetrate him, and realize him?
"O Sakka, tell me of that sage as I should know him—
explain that to me, O All-Seeing One.
"That" refers to whom I ask, whom I entreat, whom I beseech, and whom I inspire with confidence.
"Explains" means: explain, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, make clear, manifest, and illuminate.
"Omniscient eye" (samantacakkhu): the omniscient eye is said to be the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) … [as before] … the Tathāgata is called "omniscient eye" by virtue of that.
"Explain that to me, O All-Seeing One.
Therefore, that brahmin said:
"He is without hope, or perhaps still hoping..."
“Is he one possessed of wisdom,
or does he merely fashion wisdom? Sakka, tell me how I may know a sage, O All-Seeing One.”
He is without longing and does not long for anything;
he possesses wisdom and does not fashion a conceptualization of wisdom.
Know him, Todeyya, to be such a sage.
Possessing nothing, unattached to the realm of sensual existence,
free from longing and not desiring anything— he is one without craving; he does not yearn for forms.

In sounds … and so on … in odors … in mental phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, one does not long for them, does not desire them, does not approve of them, does not aspire to them, does not crave them, and does not yearn for them.
"He is without longing and does not long;
he possesses wisdom and does not fashion [a view] by means of wisdom.
Regarding "possessing wisdom": he is wise, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.

"And he does not construct with wisdom": by means of the knowledge of the eight attainments, or the knowledge of the five higher knowledges, or even wrong knowledge, he does not construct a construction of craving, nor does he construct a construction of views;
he does not produce them, does not generate them, does not bring them forth, and does not cause them to arise—thus, being possessed of wisdom, he does not construct with wisdom.
In this way too, Todeyya, one understands the sage.
"Sage" (muni): "mone" is said to be knowledge ... [as before] ... having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage.
In this way too, Todeyya, one understands the sage. Todeyya, know the sage thus; acknowledge him, penetrate him, and pierce through him.
In this way too, Todeyya, know the sage as one who possesses nothing and is unattached to sensual existence. "Possessing nothing" means:
the possession of lust, the possession of hatred, the possession of delusion, the possession of conceit, the possession of views, the possession of defilements, and the possession of misconduct.

He for whom these possessions have been abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge—he is called "one who possesses nothing" (*akiñcana*).
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures (*kāma*):
sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*). …pe…
These are called sensual pleasures as objects … [as above] … these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.
Existence is twofold: there are two kinds of existence.
Kamma-existence and rebirth-linking existence, which is renewed existence... [etc.
...this is rebirth-linking renewed existence.
"Possessing nothing, unattached to sense-existence": this refers to a person who possesses nothing and is unattached and unclinging to both sense-pleasures and existence.
Dwelling with a mind that is unattached, unimpeded, emerged, escaped, liberated, dissociated, and free from boundaries—
one who possesses nothing and is not clinging to the realm of sense-desire.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He is without longing and does not long;
he is possessed of wisdom and does not fashion wisdom.”
“Thus, Todeyya, know the sage to be one who possesses nothing and is unattached to sensual existence. At the conclusion of this verse,
…pe… [the Venerable Todeyya attained the fruit of stream-entry].
"The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This concludes the ninth exposition: The Questions of the Young Brahmin Todeyya.
